books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: This map, titled “Territory of Louisiana 1803–1819,” shows the Louisiana Purchase territory shaded red and labeled “LOUISIANA PURCHASE.” A note in the corner reads: “Louisiana Purchase Territory ceded by FRANCE to the UNITED STATES by treaty of April 30, 1803, as asserted and maintained by the American Government.” The shaded land stretches from the Mississippi River west to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico north to Canada. New Orleans sits at the mouth of the Mississippi River.
stimulus.source_note: Map of the Louisiana Purchase Territory, National Archives (NARA 594889); public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: President Jefferson's decision to buy Louisiana is best understood as an example of

options.text: a president who followed his party's strict reading of the Constitution without exception
options.misconception: A strict reading gave the president no power to buy land; Jefferson acted against his own rule.

options.text: Congress refusing to spend money on western land
options.misconception: Congress approved the purchase; the money question was Jefferson's, not Congress's refusal.

options.text: France forcing the United States to accept the whole territory
options.misconception: France offered the whole territory; Jefferson chose to take the offer, he was not forced.

options.text: a president setting aside his own constitutional doubts for a practical gain

rationales.A: Jefferson had argued for a strict reading of the Constitution, and nothing in it authorized buying land. His decision broke his own rule.
rationales.B: Congress went along with the purchase and paid the $15 million. The doubt was Jefferson's, not a congressional refusal.
rationales.C: Napoleon offered the whole territory because he needed cash and had lost Haiti. Jefferson weighed the offer and chose to accept it.
rationales.D: Jefferson believed the Constitution gave him no power to buy land, and he thought about seeking an amendment. He went ahead anyway, using his treaty power, because the land was too valuable to refuse.
rationales.general:
1. Recall Jefferson's rule. He had argued for a strict reading of the Constitution, with only the powers it names.
2. Find the gap. Nothing in the Constitution authorizes a president to buy land from another country.
3. Watch what he did. He considered an amendment, then bought Louisiana anyway under his power to make treaties.
Background: Napoleon offered the whole territory for $15 million because he needed money for war in Europe and his army in Haiti had been destroyed by disease.
Remember: when a leader breaks his own stated rule, ask what practical gain was worth the break.
